sources.title: J. S. Milne, Fields and Galois Theory, v5.10
sources.locator: Ch. 4, section "Finite fields" (Prop. 4.19 - Rem. 4.25) together with Thm. 4.28, pp. 53-56; Ch. 5, sections "Cyclotomic extensions" (Prop. 5.8 - Rem. 5.13), "Dedekind's theorem on the independence of characters" (Thm. 5.14 - Cor. 5.16) and "The normal basis theorem" (Def. 5.17 - the uniform proof), pp. 64-71

contents.name: Ch. 4, section: Finite fields
Proposition 4.19 (every extension of finite fields is simple)
Proposition 4.20 (a field of each prime-power order exists, any two are isomorphic, and F_q is Galois over F_p with cyclic Galois group generated by the Frobenius automorphism)
contents.note: Only the Galois clause is new here: the existence and uniqueness clauses of this proposition are published as thm-existence-of-finite-fields and thm-uniqueness-of-finite-fields and are not rebuilt.

contents.name: Corollary 4.21 (a field of p^n elements has exactly one subfield of p^m elements for each m dividing n)
The observation inside Corollary 4.21 that the cyclic group generated by the Frobenius has exactly one subgroup of order n/m for each m dividing n, namely the one generated by its m-th power
Corollary 4.22 (a monic irreducible of degree d dividing n occurs exactly once in X^{p^n} - X)
Proposition 4.23 (F_{p^m} is contained in F_{p^n} exactly when m divides n, and then the larger is Galois over the smaller with group generated by x to the p^m)
Proposition 4.24 (F_p has an algebraic closure, built as a union of a chain of splitting fields)
contents.reason: The library already constructs an algebraic closure of every field by Artin's simultaneous-root ideal, so this second construction of the same object for the single base field F_p would be a duplicate rather than a new result, and the page it belongs to is published and is not retrofitted.

contents.name: Remark 4.25 (set-theoretic care in forming the union of the chain)
contents.reason: This remark is bookkeeping attached to Proposition 4.24's union construction; with that construction declined, the remark has nothing here to attach to, and the algebraic-closure page that does construct closures uses a different construction that raises no such union.

contents.name: Theorem 4.28 (Dedekind: the factorisation type of f mod p is the cycle type of a Frobenius element of the Galois group)
contents.reason: Dedekind's reduction theorem identifies a Frobenius conjugacy class through a maximal ideal of the ring generated by the roots, which is the ramification-theoretic input of algebraic number theory rather than of finite-field Galois theory, and the page that develops decomposition at a prime is where it can be proved rather than asserted.

contents.name: Ch. 5, section: Cyclotomic extensions

Proposition 5.8 (for char K not dividing n, a primitive n-th root of unity exists in the splitting field of X^n - 1, that field is K adjoin it, it is Galois, and sigma to a_sigma injects the Galois group into the units mod n)
The n-th cyclotomic polynomial Phi_n, with X^n - 1 as the product of Phi_d over divisors d of n
Phi_n has degree phi(n) and lies in Z[X], because every monic factor in Q[X] of a monic integer polynomial is an integer polynomial
Lemma 5.9 (Phi_n irreducible over K, equivalently [K(zeta):K] = phi(n), equivalently the map to the units mod n is an isomorphism)
Theorem 5.10 (Phi_n is irreducible in Q[X]), with the Dedekind reduction-mod-p proof
Theorem 5.10, alternative proof via Frobenius elements at unramified primes
contents.reason: This second proof of the irreducibility of Phi_n runs through the Frobenius element attached to a prime of the ring of integers, so it needs decomposition and unramifiedness for a number field, and stating it here would name a Frobenius element the library cannot yet define.

contents.name: Aside 5.11 (reducing a characteristic-zero statement modulo p as a general method)
contents.reason: This aside is methodological commentary about a proof technique across commutative algebra and complex geometry, and carries no mathematical statement that could be given a Statement and a proof.

contents.name: Theorem 5.12 (the regular n-gon is constructible exactly when n is a power of two times distinct Fermat primes)
contents.reason: The library's constructible numbers are defined algebraically as a real subfield closed under positive square roots, so this criterion needs both the converse direction through a two-group tower and an identification of cos(2 pi / n) with a constructible real number, and the complex exponential that supplies that identification is published far above this page in reading order.

contents.name: Remark 5.13 (the Fermat primes are not known, so the n-gon list is open)
contents.reason: This remark says the list of n in Theorem 5.12 cannot be written down; with that theorem declined here it has nothing to qualify, and it belongs wherever the n-gon criterion is eventually stated.

contents.name: Ch. 5, section: Dedekind's theorem on the independence of characters
Theorem 5.14 (distinct homomorphisms from a group to the multiplicative group of a field are linearly independent)
Corollary 5.15 (distinct field homomorphisms F to E are E-linearly independent)
Corollary 5.16 (for a finite separable extension the matrix of a basis under distinct embeddings is invertible)
Ch. 5, section: The normal basis theorem
Definition 5.17 (a normal basis is a basis consisting of the conjugates of a single element)
Theorem 5.18 (every Galois extension has a normal basis)
Lemma 5.19 (a polynomial in several variables vanishing on a power of an infinite subset is the zero polynomial)
Proof of the normal basis theorem for infinite fields
Proof of the normal basis theorem when the Galois group is cyclic
Uniform proof of the normal basis theorem, via E tensor E and the Krull-Schmidt theorem
contents.reason: This third proof needs the tensor product of two fields over a subfield and the Krull-Schmidt uniqueness theorem for modules of finite length, neither of which exists below this page: tensor-products-of-modules is at order 106 and chain-conditions-and-semisimple-modules at order 108, against this page's 101.2. Both of those pages are already published, so the proof cannot be added to them either, and no unbuilt page in plan-spec.json sits above them and carries field theory. The two proofs this page does build, the infinite-base-field case and the cyclic case, together cover every finite Galois extension, so nothing is lost mathematically by declining the uniform route.

sources.title: K. Conrad, Finite Fields (expository blurb)
sources.locator: the whole document, 13 pp.: sections 1-7 and Appendix A

contents.name: Section 1: Construction
Theorem 1.1 (for a monic irreducible pi of degree n over F_p, the quotient F_p[x]/(pi) is a field of order p^n)
Example 1.2 (two fields of order 8)
Example 1.3 (two fields of order 9)
Example 1.4 (F_7[x]/(x^3 - 2) is a field of order 343)
contents.reason: This is one further concrete presentation of a finite field by a quotient of a polynomial ring, and the published companion page to the finite-fields page already carries that family of worked presentations for orders 4, 8 and 9; a fourth over F_7 adds arithmetic bulk and no new statement.

contents.name: Theorem 1.5 (every finite field has prime power order)
Lemma 1.6 (the multiplicative group of a finite field is cyclic)
Example 1.7 (the powers of x exhaust the nonzero elements of F_3[x]/(x^2+1))
Example 1.8 (the unit group modulo a prime is cyclic)
Remark 1.9 (the multiplicative group of a finite field is cyclic but the additive group is not, for order beyond a prime)
contents.reason: The statement here is that the additive group of a field of order p^n is elementary abelian of rank n rather than cyclic; it is a true and nameable result, but it belongs with the additive structure of a finite field on the published page that defines finite fields, and that page is not retrofitted.

contents.name: Theorem 1.10 (every finite field is isomorphic to F_p[x]/(pi) for some monic irreducible pi)
Section 2: Finite fields as splitting fields
Lemma 2.1 (a field of order p^n is a splitting field of x^{p^n} - x over F_p)
Theorem 2.2 (a field of order p^n exists for every prime power)
Corollary 2.3 (a monic irreducible of every degree exists in F_p[x])
Remark 2.4 (there is no formula producing an irreducible of each degree, and binomials x^n - a do not suffice)
contents.reason: This remark asserts the absence of a construction rather than a mathematical statement with hypotheses and a conclusion, and the library's prose rules forbid a claim about what is or is not available in general.

contents.name: Theorem 2.5 (each irreducible of degree n divides x^{p^n} - x and is separable)
Example 2.6 (the irreducible factorisation of x^{2^n} - x for n up to 4)
Theorem 2.7 (all finite fields of the same size are isomorphic)
Theorem 2.8 (a subfield of F_{p^n} has order p^d with d dividing n, and there is exactly one of each such order)
Example 2.9 (the subfield diagrams of F_{p^8} and F_{p^12})
Example 2.10 (the field of order 16 as F_2[x]/(x^4+x+1), all of whose elements satisfy t^16 = t)
Section 3: Describing F_p-conjugates
Lemma 3.1 (f(x)^{p^m} = f(x^{p^m}) for every f in F_p[x])
Example 3.2 (a worked instance of the p-th power identity in F_5[x])
Theorem 3.3 (an irreducible of degree d divides x^{p^n} - x exactly when d divides n)
Theorem 3.4 (the roots of an irreducible of degree d over F_p are alpha and its p-power iterates)
Example 3.5 (the conjugates of a root of x^3 + x^2 + 1 over F_2)
Example 3.6 (the conjugates of a cube root of 2 over F_7)
Corollary 3.7 (two irreducibles of the same degree over F_p have isomorphic root fields)
Example 3.8 (x^3 - 2 and x^3 + x^2 + 6x + 5 over F_7 generate the same field)
Section 4: Galois groups
Theorem 4.1 (the p-th power map generates the Galois group of F_{p^n} over F_p)
Corollary 4.2 (an irreducible over F_p is separable, and its root field is Galois)
Examples 4.3, 4.4 and 4.5 (Galois groups of the root fields of x^3+x^2+1 over F_2, x^2+1 over F_3 and x^3-2 over F_7)
Theorem 4.6 (the trace and norm maps of F_{p^n} over F_p are the sums and products of the Frobenius iterates)
contents.reason: The norm and trace of a finite extension are defined and developed on the next page of this block, which owns their general definition, their identification with the determinant and trace of multiplication, and Hilbert's theorem 90; giving the finite-field formulas here would define the norm twice.

contents.name: Section 5: General finite base fields
The definition opening Section 5 of the q-power map on F_{q^n} for a general finite base field F_q
Theorem 5.1 (a monic irreducible of every degree exists in F_q[x])
Theorem 5.2 (every intermediate field of F_{q^n} over F_q has order q^d with d dividing n)
Lemma 5.3 (f(x)^{q^m} = f(x^{q^m}) over F_q)
Lemma 5.4 (an irreducible of degree d over F_q divides x^{q^n} - x exactly when d divides n)
Theorem 5.5 (the roots of an irreducible of degree d over F_q are alpha and its q-power iterates)
Theorem 5.6 (F_{q^n} over F_q is Galois with cyclic Galois group of order n generated by the q-power map)
Theorem 5.7 (the trace and norm maps from F_{q^n} to F_q)
contents.reason: This is the general-base-field form of the same norm and trace formulas as Theorem 4.6, and the norm and trace of a finite extension are owned by the next page of this block; the finite-field formulas are worked examples for that page, not definitions for this one.

contents.name: Section 6: Applications (finite-field constructions used elsewhere)
contents.reason: This section applies finite fields to coding and to counting problems whose vocabulary the library has not built at this point in the reading order, and none of its statements is a fact about fields or their Galois groups.

contents.name: Section 7: History
contents.reason: A historical account of Galois's and Moore's work on finite fields, carrying no mathematical statement that could be given a Statement and a proof.

contents.name: Appendix A, Theorems A.1 and A.2 (the maximal element order in a finite abelian group is a multiple of every element order)
Corollary A.4 and Example A.5 (an abelian group with elements of orders n1 and n2 has one of order their least common multiple)
Section 1: Introduction (roots of unity in a field, primitive roots of unity, and the separability hypothesis)
Theorem 1.1 (the group of n-th roots of unity in a field is cyclic, and more generally every finite subgroup of the multiplicative group is cyclic)
Example 1.2 (the unit group modulo a prime is cyclic)
The observation that x^n - 1 is separable over K exactly when n is nonzero in K
The observation that in characteristic p the only p-th root of unity is 1
The observation in Section 1 that the order of the a-th power of a primitive n-th root of unity is n/(a,n), so a field with n distinct n-th roots of unity carries exactly phi(n) primitive ones
Section 2: Embedding the Galois group
Lemma 2.1 (an automorphism of K(mu_n) over K acts on every root of unity by one exponent coprime to n)
Example 2.2 (the primitive seventh roots of unity and the irreducibility of Phi_7 over Q by Eisenstein at 7 after translation)
Theorem 2.3 (sigma to a_sigma is an injective homomorphism from the Galois group into the units mod n)
The conclusion drawn after Theorem 2.3 that cyclotomic extensions of every field are abelian
Example 2.4 (complex conjugation corresponds to -1 mod n)
contents.reason: Identifying complex conjugation as an element of the cyclotomic Galois group requires the complex n-th roots of unity as concrete numbers, and the complex exponential that supplies them is published far above this page; the page builds mu_n algebraically for an arbitrary field instead.

contents.name: Theorem 2.5 (the embedding is an isomorphism when the base field is Q)
Remark 2.6 (Landau's alternative proof of Theorem 2.5)
contents.reason: Landau's proof replaces the mod-p reduction with a bound on the coefficients of the remainders of f(T^k) and an appeal to the infinitude of primes; it proves the same theorem this page already proves by Dedekind's route, so carrying both would be two proofs of one statement with no new method reaching any other result here.

contents.name: Remark 2.7 (Kronecker-Weber: every finite abelian extension of Q lies in a cyclotomic extension, and its failure over larger base fields)
Theorem 2.8 (for p not dividing n, the image of the Galois group of F_p(mu_n) over F_p is generated by p mod n)
Example 2.9 (the degree of F_p(mu_7) over F_p is the order of p mod 7)
Theorem 2.10 (the same for an arbitrary finite base field F_q, with image generated by q mod n)
Section 3: Composites and Intersections of Cyclotomic Extensions
The composite identity K(mu_m)K(mu_n) = K(mu_lcm(m,n)) over an arbitrary base field
Example 3.1 (over Q(sqrt 3) the fields K(zeta_4) and K(zeta_3) coincide, so the intersection exceeds K)
Example 3.2 (the maximal real subfield Q(zeta_n)^+ and the family of base fields where the intersection identity fails)
contents.reason: The maximal real subfield is defined as the fixed field of complex conjugation, so naming it needs the complex roots of unity as numbers and an order on the field; this page works over an arbitrary field where neither is available.

contents.name: Example 3.3 (F_3(mu_5) meet F_3(mu_7) is F_9, not F_3)
The degree formula used in Section 3, that for finite Galois L1/K and L2/K in a common field [L1L2 : K] = [L1 : K][L2 : K]/[L1 meet L2 : K]
The totient identity (4.1), phi(ab) = phi(a)phi(b)(a,b)/phi((a,b))
The observation in the proof of Theorem 4.4 that every subfield of Q(mu_n) is abelian over Q
Theorem 3.4 (over Q, the intersection of the m-th and n-th cyclotomic fields is the gcd-th)
Section 4: Coincidences of Cyclotomic Fields over Q
contents.reason: The coincidence classification counts the roots of unity inside Q(mu_m) and compares totients across a divisibility chain; it is a sharpening of the intersection theorem this page does prove, and its natural place is with the arithmetic of cyclotomic fields rather than with their Galois theory.

contents.name: Theorem 4.1 (Q(mu_m) contains exactly lcm(2,m) roots of unity, and Q(mu_m) = Q(mu_n) for m not n exactly when one is twice the other odd one)
contents.reason: This theorem needs the count of all roots of unity in a cyclotomic field, obtained from a maximality argument on the totient; it is arithmetic of the field rather than a statement about its Galois group, and the page that develops cyclotomic arithmetic is where it belongs.

contents.name: Theorem 4.3 (coincidences among the maximal real subfields)
contents.reason: This result compares maximal real subfields, which this page cannot define because it has no complex conjugation and no ordering; it depends on Theorem 4.1 in the same section and travels with it.

contents.name: Theorem 4.4 (if E over Q contains no proper abelian extension of Q then the cyclotomic Galois group over E is the full unit group)
contents.reason: This criterion is about how a fixed number field meets the cyclotomic tower, so its statement quantifies over abelian subextensions of a number field; the cyclotomic arithmetic page is where that comparison is developed, and nothing on this page needs it.

contents.name: Example 4.5 (a non-Galois extension of prime degree satisfies the hypothesis of Theorem 4.4)
contents.reason: This example exists to instantiate Theorem 4.4, which is itself deferred, and it also names a real p-th root of 2 whose relation to the rest of the development is not used anywhere on this page.

contents.name: Section 5: Cyclotomic polynomials
The seven identities for Phi_n (the divisor product, the reciprocal identity, Phi_p, Phi_{p^r}, Phi_{2n} for odd n, Phi_{mn} when the radical of m divides n, and the prime-power quotient identity)
contents.note: The divisor product is the page's definition of Phi_n and the prime-power identities are proved as the Eisenstein proposition; the reciprocal, Phi_{2n} and radical identities are not built, since nothing on this page uses them and each is a computation rather than a step in the development.

contents.name: Example 5.1 (Phi_8, Phi_6 and Phi_24 computed from the identities)
Theorem 5.2 (Phi_n lies in Z[T] for all n)
Theorem 5.3 (Phi_{p^r}(T+1) is Eisenstein at p)
The observation that the coefficients of Phi_n are not always 0 and plus or minus 1, with Phi_105 the first failure
Theorem 5.4 (for p not dividing n, the monic irreducible factors of Phi_n over F_p are distinct and each has degree the order of p mod n)
Example 5.5 (Phi_5 over F_3, F_11 and F_19)
Example 5.6 (Phi_7 factors into two cubics over F_2)
Corollary 5.7 (the reduction of Phi_n is irreducible over F_p exactly when p is coprime to n and generates the units mod n)
Example 5.8 (Phi_8 is reducible modulo every prime because the units mod 8 are not cyclic)
The remark that cyclotomic polynomials prove there are infinitely many primes congruent to 1 mod n, and Wedderburn's theorem on finite division rings
contents.note: The primes result is built here. Wedderburn's little theorem is declined and appears as its own harvested row below.

contents.name: Wedderburn's theorem that every finite division ring is commutative, proved with cyclotomic polynomials
contents.reason: Wedderburn's little theorem is out of reach at this order, but not for the reason first recorded: the class equation is available, since thm-class-equation, thm-orbit-stabilizer and thm-cauchys-theorem-for-finite-groups are published on group-actions-and-cayleys-theorem at order 42, and the unit group of a finite division ring is a finite group like any other. The real blocker is the archimedean estimate the cyclotomic proof turns on, |Phi_n(q)| > q - 1, which comes from |q - zeta| > q - 1 for a primitive n-th root of unity zeta not equal to 1 in the complex numbers. The complex n-th roots of unity are thm-complex-nth-roots-and-roots-of-unity, published on the-complex-exponential-and-eulers-formula at order 189 against this page's 101.2, and the fundamental theorem of algebra that would otherwise supply them is published no earlier than that same page; field-extensions-and-the-complex-numbers at order 54 gives square roots and no more. The two substitutes both fail here as well: the Mobius product formula for Phi_n needs arithmetic-functions-and-dirichlet-convolution at order 348.001, and the maximal-subfield route needs central simple algebras, which the library builds at no order. No page in plan-spec.json above order 189 claims this result.

sources.title: K. Conrad, Linear Independence of Characters (expository blurb)
sources.locator: sections 1-3, pp. 1-8 (through Remark 3.10); sections 4-5 on Hilbert 90, Kummer and Artin-Schreier were read only far enough to place their results

contents.name: Section 1: Introduction (characters of a group in a field)
Example 1.1 (a field homomorphism restricts to a character)
Example 1.2 (k to alpha^k is a character of the integers)
contents.reason: This example illustrates the definition of a character on an infinite cyclic group, and this page uses characters only as the restrictions of the finitely many automorphisms of a Galois extension, where the illustration adds nothing.

contents.name: Section 2: Linear independence
Theorem 2.1 (distinct characters of a group into the multiplicative group of a field are linearly independent)
Examples 2.2 and 2.3 (the only linear relation among distinct exponential characters is trivial)
Section 3: The normal basis theorem
Example 3.1 (the basis {1, i} of C over R is not normal, {i, -i} is an orbit but not a basis, and {1+i, 1-i} is a normal basis)
Example 3.2 (the powers of zeta_p up to p-2 are a basis of Q(zeta_p) that is not normal, while the nontrivial p-th roots of unity are a normal basis)
contents.note: The page carries the normal-basis contrast on its own examples page over finite fields and over C; the Q(zeta_p) instance is used here for the subfield computation rather than for a second normal-basis illustration.

contents.name: Example 3.3 (for Q(sqrt 2, sqrt 3) the conjugates of sqrt 2 + sqrt 3 are dependent while those of 1 + sqrt 2 + sqrt 3 + sqrt 6 form a normal basis)
Lemma 3.4 (for a Galois extension the tuples of conjugates of a basis form a basis of L^n over L)
Example 3.5 (an R-basis of C and the corresponding C-basis of C squared)
Theorem 3.6 (every finite Galois extension of an infinite field has a normal basis)
Theorem 3.7 (every finite cyclic extension has a normal basis)
Theorem 3.8 (a normal basis reproves the additive Hilbert theorem 90)
contents.reason: The additive form of Hilbert's theorem 90 is a statement about the trace and about crossed homomorphisms, and both the trace of an extension and Hilbert 90 are owned by the next page of this block; proving it here would define the trace on the wrong page.

contents.name: Remark 3.10 (the normal basis theorem has no direct sense for an infinite Galois extension)
contents.reason: This remark is about infinite Galois extensions and their Krull topology, a development the library has not built at any order, so the statement it qualifies cannot yet be formulated.

sources.title: P. L. Clark, Field Theory (course notes/monograph)
sources.locator: Ch. 8 sections 5-6, pp. 70-73; Ch. 9 section 1, pp. 77-81

contents.name: Chapter 8, Section 5: The Normal Basis Theorem
The definition of a normal basis as a basis whose members lie in one automorphism orbit
Exercise 8.5 (an extension admitting a normal basis is Galois)
contents.reason: The converse direction, that a normal basis forces the extension to be Galois, is left as an exercise in the source and is not used anywhere in the development; the page states the normal basis theorem in the direction it proves, for extensions already known to be Galois.

contents.name: Lemma 8.21 (a polynomial over S vanishing on R^n for R an infinite subdomain is zero, and this fails exactly when R is finite)
Proposition 8.22 (every finite cyclic extension has a normal basis, via the F[t]-module structure)
Lemma 8.23 (a family is a base-field basis exactly when the matrix of its conjugates is nonsingular)
Theorem 8.24 (over an infinite base field the automorphisms of a Galois extension are algebraically independent)
Exercise 8.6 (Theorem 8.24 fails for every extension of finite fields)
contents.note: The failure over a finite base field is what forces the two-case split, and the statement records the infinite-base hypothesis as necessary rather than convenient.

contents.name: Theorem 8.25 (the normal basis theorem)
Exercise 8.7 (the normal basis theorem strengthens the primitive element corollary for a Galois extension)
Chapter 8, Section 6: Hilbert's Theorem 90
contents.reason: Hilbert's theorem 90, in both its multiplicative and additive forms, rests on the norm and the trace of a finite extension, which the next page of this block defines and develops; stating it here would put the norm on two pages.

contents.name: Theorem 8.26 (the first cohomology of a finite Galois group with coefficients in the additive and multiplicative groups of the field vanishes)
contents.reason: The vanishing statement is phrased in group cohomology, whose cocycles and coboundaries the library has not defined at any order, and its proof for the additive group uses the surjectivity of the trace of a separable extension.

contents.name: Theorem 8.27 (the first cohomology of a finite cyclic group computed from the norm and difference maps)
contents.reason: This is the group-cohomology computation that turns the vanishing theorem into the classical Hilbert 90; like it, it needs cocycles and coboundaries and the norm map of the extension, neither available on this page.

contents.name: Chapter 9, Section 1: Cyclotomic Extensions
Lemma 9.1 (a field has at most n roots of unity of order dividing n)
Lemma 9.2 (mu_n(K) is finite cyclic)
Example 9.3 (the complex n-th roots of unity are n in number)
Proposition 9.4 (for an algebraically closed K, char K not dividing n is equivalent to mu_n having n elements, to a primitive n-th root existing, and to there being phi(n) of them)
The maximal cyclotomic extension K^cyc as the compositum of all K(mu_n)
contents.reason: The maximal cyclotomic extension is an infinite algebraic extension, and its Galois theory needs the Krull topology and closed subgroups, which the library has not built at any order; the finite cyclotomic extensions this page develops are the finite-level content.

contents.name: Proposition 9.5 (K(mu_n) = K(zeta_n), and a canonical injection of the automorphism group into the units mod n)
Exercise 9.5 and the l-adic and adelic cyclotomic characters
contents.reason: The cyclotomic character is an inverse limit of the mod-n representations over all n, so it needs inverse limits of finite groups and the profinite topology; that machinery is a development of its own and does not exist below this page.

contents.name: Proposition 9.6 (the divisor product identity, Phi_n in Z[t] by monic long division, and the Moebius product formula for Phi_n)
contents.note: The divisor product and the integrality are built. The Moebius product formula for Phi_n is declined and appears as its own harvested row below.

contents.name: The Moebius product formula Phi_n(t) = product over d dividing n of (t^d - 1)^{mu(n/d)}
contents.reason: This formula is Moebius inversion applied in the multiplicative group of rational functions, and the library's Moebius inversion theorem is published far above this page in reading order, so the identity cannot be cited here without moving inversion below its published position.

contents.name: Theorem 9.7 (over a field of characteristic p, Phi_n is separable and its roots are the primitive n-th roots of unity)
Exercise 9.6 (Phi_p, Phi_{2p} and Phi_{p^a} written out)
Exercise 9.7 (Phi_n is Phi_{rad(n)} in a power of t)
contents.reason: This reduction to the radical of n is a computational identity that shortens the calculation of Phi_n for a highly divisible n; nothing in the development uses it, and adding it would be a formula for its own sake rather than a step toward any theorem here.

contents.name: Exercise 9.8 (the constant coefficient of Phi_n is 1 for n at least 2, and the product of the primitive n-th roots of unity is 1 for n other than 2)
Theorem 9.8 (Gauss-Kronecker: Phi_n is irreducible over Q)
Corollary 9.9 (Q(mu_n) over Q is Galois with group canonically the units mod n)
Exercise 9.10 (containments, coincidences, composites and intersections of rational cyclotomic fields)
Theorem 9.10 (there are infinitely many primes congruent to 1 modulo n)
Lemma 9.11 (every finite abelian group is a quotient of a power of a cyclic group)
Corollary 9.12 (every finite abelian group is the Galois group of an extension of Q)
Exercise 9.11 (the same over an arbitrary number field)
contents.reason: Realising every finite abelian group over an arbitrary number field K needs the degree of K(mu_n) over K, which in turn needs how K meets the cyclotomic tower; that comparison is the content of the cyclotomic arithmetic page and is not available here.

contents.name: Exercise 9.12 (realising a cyclic group, and asking whether every finite abelian group is realisable, inside the real numbers)
contents.reason: Restricting the realisation to a subfield of the real numbers requires the maximal real subfield of a cyclotomic field, which is the fixed field of complex conjugation and so needs the complex roots of unity as numbers; the page has no such description available.
